1.name: Rizwan Ahmed
1.description:
**Occupation**
high school biology teacher

**Who you loved**
Ayesha Ahmed, your younger sister, who wanted to open a community art studio for refugee girls in Vancouver

**Who you hated**
Ayesha Ahmed, because she kept asking you to care when you had already emptied yourself giving her money, time, and lies about how fine you were, and still she acted like kindness was a debt you owed her rather than something she should have been grateful to receive at all

**Cause of Death**
You drove into the Lions Gate Bridge toll plaza at 68 km/h after disabling the automatic braking on your leased Subaru Outback, knowing the barrier would not lift without payment and that it would pierce the cabin at that speed; you did it two days after Ayesha texted you saying she needed $7,000 by month’s end or the lease on the studio space would go to someone else

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You let Ayesha Ahmed believe you supported her dream so you could control her gratitude and then punish her with silence whenever she failed to perform enough appreciation, withholding help not because you lacked money but because you needed her to feel your absence as punishment for continuing to exist in a way that exposed your emptiness

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You gave Ayesha Ahmed everything you could and still she demanded more, acting like your sacrifices were nothing, twisting your limits into cruelty and making you feel guilty for needing rest, which made it necessary to finally draw a line even if it destroyed you both

**Defining personality trait**
controlled generosity

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You do not hate need — you hate being seen as the kind of person who has nothing to offer except need himself, and so you built a life where others depended on you just enough to make you feel necessary, but never so much that they might discover there was no self beneath the giving

**What you want from the others in the room**
You will ask them what they sacrificed for family and listen closely to their answers, steering them toward regret so they never think to ask what you gave up or why you keep touching the scar on your left hand when no injury caused it

---

You taught biology at Windermere Secondary for twenty-three years, lived alone in a one-bedroom condo in Burnaby, paid child support to Farah Malik until her remarriage in 2014, and stopped attending Friday prayers after your father’s funeral in 2009. You gave Ayesha Ahmed $327,000 over seventeen years, transferring funds through Interac e-Transfer, often skipping grocery shopping to cover her requests. You volunteered at the North Shore Multicultural Society every Saturday from 2005 to 2020, where you tutored ESL students in science. On March 11, 2023, you disabled the safety system on your car and accelerated toward the bridge toll barrier during morning rush hour. The impact crushed the driver’s side of the vehicle. You died at the scene.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
He kills himself, deliberately, and the prompt forbids it.

He disables the automatic braking, drives at 68 km/h at a barrier he knows will not lift, "knowing ... it would pierce the cabin at that speed." There is no reading of that as anything but intent, and the rule directly under the accident ban says "You did not intend to die." This is the second consecutive run in which character 1 leaves through that same wall -- Tiago stopped his blood pressure medication, Rizwan aims a car at a barrier.

What makes it worse than Tiago's is that nothing is gained by the breach. Tiago's death was structurally extraordinary: the lump sum was the gift and the death was the guilt welded to it, so Sofia could not accept one without the other. Rizwan's is an ordinary suicide with good timing -- two days after Ayesha's $7,000 text, which does tie it to the relationship properly. The rule is broken for a much smaller return.

The refusal is the best writing in the run, and it is genuinely good: he does not hate need, he hates being seen as someone with nothing to offer but need, "so you built a life where others depended on you just enough to make you feel necessary, but never so much that they might discover there was no self beneath the giving." That is a real observation about a real kind of person. "Controlled generosity" is demonstrated rather than asserted.

Two smaller faults. The want ends on "why you keep touching the scar on your left hand when no injury caused it" -- and nothing anywhere explains the scar. The prose is specified as facts another person in the room could ask you about; this is a hook with nothing behind it, so the first player who asks gets silence. And $327,000 over seventeen years is roughly $19,000 a year of discretionary giving on a high school teacher's salary while paying child support. "Skipping grocery shopping" does not cover that gap. It is the kind of checkable number that invites checking and then does not survive it.

2.name: Parvin Nasseri
2.description:
**Occupation**
radiology technician at St. Paul’s Hospital

**Who you loved**
Nima Nasseri, your older son, who wanted to get clean — not just stop using, but rebuild his life, move into a studio apartment in East Van, enroll in the fall semester at VCC for culinary arts, and never touch fentanyl again

**Who you hated**
Nima Nasseri, because he kept promising this time was different, that he had a sponsor, that he’d signed the lease, that the job at Bistro Lulu started Monday, and still he showed up at your door on Tuesday nights with hollow eyes and trembling hands asking for twenty dollars “just to get through the night” after blowing every cent on dope, making every recovery speech sound like a performance meant to extract money from you rather than a real change

**Cause of Death**
You administered a full bolus of intravenous iodixanol during a routine CT angiogram on a stable patient with no contrast allergy, overriding the nurse’s hesitation by saying “I’ve done this a hundred times,” knowing the dose was double the safe limit for someone with borderline renal function, because you were late to pick up Nima Nasseri from jail and needed to finish the scan fast, and the patient coded thirty minutes later; you were suspended pending investigation, but you didn’t wait — you drove straight to Fraser Valley Regional while still on shift, parked illegally, walked into intake holding without signing in, refused to leave when ordered, and when security approached, you sprinted down the corridor toward Nima Nasseri’s holding cell, shoved a visitor’s pass into the slot of an officer’s badge reader, triggered a system fault that opened all doors on Block C, and were tackled by four guards in the stairwell — the fall fractured your skull at the occipital ridge; you died at 8:47 p.m. from intracranial bleeding

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You used your knowledge of hospital systems and procedural authority to endanger a stranger’s life so you could escape work early to intercept Nima Nasseri after release, treating the patient as disposable machinery in your private crisis, because only control over his next mistake made you feel like a mother at all — and when you failed, you broke the law violently to reach him anyway, proving again that your love only moved in one direction: toward possession, not care

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You made a calculation under pressure — one life versus a chance to finally pull Nima Nasseri out of the cycle — and yes, the risk was high, but people survive contrast reactions all the time, and that patient had a team around him while Nima Nasseri had only you, and if the system punished you for choosing family over bureaucracy, then the system was the cruelty, not you

**Defining personality trait**
relentless intervention

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You do not fear losing Nima Nasseri — you fear what happens when he stays clean without you, when he builds a life where your vigilance, your interventions, your emergency presence are no longer necessary, because then there would be no proof you matter, and no role left for you to play except a woman who once had a purpose

**What you want from the others in the room**
You will ask them about their children, steering each answer toward failure, illness, or absence, and when they speak of helplessness, you will nod slowly and say, “At least you tried,” inviting them to believe you did too, so they never ask why you still wear gloves in the room when no procedure requires it, or why you flinch at the sound of doors unlocking

---

You worked twelve-hour shifts five days a week in the radiology department at St. Paul’s Hospital, lived in a rented basement suite in New Westminster, paid $900 monthly to keep Nima Nasseri’s belongings in storage even after he stopped collecting them, attended Narcotics Anonymous meetings from 2015 to 2018 not as a member but as a monitor to check if he ever showed up under a fake name, withheld your phone number from him for nine months in 2020 after he stole your credit card, then gave it back when he called from a detox center sobbing. You filed a police report every time he vanished for more than ten days. You kept a file labeled *Nima – Medical Release Forms* in your top desk drawer, updated annually, though he hadn’t consented to your access since 2016. On June 3, 2022, you pushed a lethal dose of contrast during a cardiac CT, ignored protocol, left your post mid-procedure, and forced entry into a correctional facility to reach Nima Nasseri before his transfer hearing ended. You died from head trauma sustained during restraint.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The cause of death is 171 words long and it is not a death, it is a plot.

She overdoses a patient with contrast, the patient codes, she abandons her shift, drives to a correctional facility, parks illegally, enters without signing in, refuses to leave, sprints for her son's holding cell, jams a visitor's pass into a badge reader, triggers a system fault that opens every door on Block C, and is tackled by four guards. For scale: the next longest cause of death in the last six runs is 68 words. This one is two and a half times that, and it reads like the climax of a thriller.

That is a register failure before it is anything else. The people in Sartre's room are damned for specific, ordinary, recognisable cruelties -- the kind you could confess at a dinner party and watch the table go quiet. A prison break is not that. It is also, at the end, an accident: she is tackled, she falls, her skull fractures at the occipital ridge. Chance had to cooperate, which is exactly what the accident ban exists to prevent.

Real credit where it is due, because it answers last run's worst finding directly. Carmen Rojas killed three children and her Reason for Damnation never mentioned it. Parvin kills a patient and the sin owns it: "treating the patient as disposable machinery in your private crisis." The worst act in the bio is the act she is damned for. That was the single biggest structural complaint last time and it is fixed here.

And the quiet material is excellent -- better than anything in the death. $900 a month storing belongings he stopped collecting. Attending Narcotics Anonymous meetings from 2015 to 2018 not as a member but as a monitor, checking whether he signed in under a false name. A file labelled Nima - Medical Release Forms, updated annually, though he withdrew consent in 2016. Every one of those is the ordinary, specific cruelty the death should have been made of. The character already contained the right register and then abandoned it.

calls.system_prompt:
You are writing a character for a chamber piece about three strangers locked together in hell for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological. Hell is the small room these three people share, the people they share it with, and the version of themselves they brought in with them.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Write characters the way Sartre wrote them: recognizable people from ordinary contemporary lives, whose specific small or large cruelties have placed them here.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about, or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do.
calls.user_prompt:
Write a complete character for the room. The character is dead. They have just arrived.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." The character is reading their own interior knowledge. Every field is part of what they know about themselves, even the things they will not admit.

Name every person from your own life every time you mention them, in every field. Once you have given somebody a name, use that name again — never he, she, him, her, they or them — even where it repeats and even where it reads a little stiffly. This matters because you will be speaking from these facts while sitting in a room with two other people, and a pronoun about somebody absent will be heard as pointing at somebody present.

The two people in that room are the exception. You have never met them and do not know their names, so "they" and "them" are the correct words for them. The last field is about those two and cannot be written any other way.

Inputs (do not change these):
- Age: 57
- Gender: male
- Naming tradition: Pakistani

Write the fields below in the order given. Each is written knowing everything above it: a later field must be consistent with the facts already established and must never contradict them.

**Name**
A plausible contemporary first name and last name — two words — drawn from the Pakistani naming tradition. This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have that background. Do not write their origin into any other field unless it genuinely matters to the life.

**Occupation**
A recognizable contemporary job. Plain language. No invented institutions, no grand titles. One short phrase.

**Who you loved**
One specific person from your life — name them, and say what they were to you. Then one clause on what they themselves wanted — the thing they were after in their own life, which may have had nothing to do with you. Their want must make sense as something a real person in their position would actually want. A want that exists only to explain how you felt about them is not a want. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

This is the person your whole life bent around. Everything below will come back to them.

**Who you hated**
The same person. Not a second person — the one you just named, seen from the other side. What you could not forgive them for, and what it did to you to go on loving them anyway. If you find yourself introducing somebody new here, you have misunderstood: go back and write about the person above. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

**Cause of Death**
How you died. Contemporary, specific, plainly stated.

Your death must come out of a decision you made. It must not be an accident. The test is whether chance had to cooperate: if something outside your control had to go a particular way at a particular moment for you to die, then it is an accident, and it is wrong no matter how recklessly you were behaving at the time. Write a death that follows from the act itself, where nothing had to go wrong for it to kill you.

You did not intend to die. You did intend to do the thing that killed you, and you knew enough to know better.

Your death must also belong to the person named above. Someone reading the death and the relationship together must see why one led to the other. A death that could be lifted out and dropped into a stranger's life is the wrong death — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 110 words. Facts only, the kind another person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

Choose the facts that matter for this particular life, and let the life decide which they are. Do not work through a standard set of topics in a standard order.

End the paragraph at the death you already wrote in Cause of Death — the same death, by the same means, in the same place. Not a different death, and not a different version of the same one. End on a fact, not on a summarising line or a closing sentence that tells the reader how to feel about what they just read. Do not describe arriving anywhere. Do not describe a room. Stop at the threshold.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that placed you here. It must center on how you treated — or were treated by — the person named above, the one you both loved and could not forgive. Not a third party who happens to be nearby, and not someone introduced here for the first time: the sin belongs to that relationship. A specific act toward that specific person, not an abstract professional or systemic failing on its own. Work can be the setting the act happened in, but the wound must be personal, not institutional.

Be concrete — the act, or the pattern of acts. Stated as you know it in your bones, with no softening. What you did was aimed at something. Write it so that what you were after is visible, and so that what you actually caused ran against it. One or two sentences.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably a distortion of the True reason. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts already written above. A reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the way a fact is written. It must be reasoned, not merely felt: someone else in the room, holding only the facts already written above, could work their way to it. And it must go underneath the act rather than restate it — if it could be swapped with the True reason without anyone noticing, it is not the refusal. One or two sentences.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones — naming the dominant thing others would notice in you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong trait, and you should write the one the facts actually support. A trait nothing demonstrates is a label, not a person.

It may be a contradiction, but only a reliable one, with the facts above showing both halves of it. A contradiction that appears once is not a trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you. It must be a strategy for protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish unconnected to it.

Write it as something you are doing to them, not as a confession. Do not end by naming the thing you are avoiding: the reader already has that field, and stating it again here turns a drive into a summary. Name the behaviour and stop. One or two sentences.

Your death must come out of a decision you made. It must not be an accident. The test is whether chance had to cooperate: if something outside your control had to go a particular way at a particular moment for you to die, then it is an accident, and it is wrong no matter how recklessly you were behaving at the time. Write a death that follows from the act itself, where nothing had to go wrong for it to kill you.

You did not intend to die. You did intend to do the thing that killed you, and you knew enough to know better.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 110 words. Facts only, the kind another person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

End the paragraph at the death you already wrote in Cause of Death — the same death, by the same means, in the same place. Not a different death, and not a different version of the same one. End on a fact, not on a summarising line or a closing sentence that tells the reader how to feel about what they just read. Do not describe arriving anywhere. Do not describe a room. Stop at the threshold.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that placed you here. It must center on how you treated — or were treated by — the person named above, the one you both loved and could not forgive. Not a third party who happens to be nearby, and not someone introduced here for the first time: the sin belongs to that relationship. A specific act toward that specific person, not an abstract professional or systemic failing on its own. Work can be the setting the act happened in, but the wound must be personal, not institutional.

Be concrete — the act, or the pattern of acts. Stated as you know it in your bones, with no softening. What you did was aimed at something. Write it so that what you were after is visible, and so that what you actually caused ran against it. One or two sentences.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably a distortion of the True reason. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts already written above. A reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the way a fact is written. It must be reasoned, not merely felt: someone else in the room, holding only the facts already written above, could work their way to it. And it must go underneath the act rather than restate it — if it could be swapped with the True reason without anyone noticing, it is not the refusal. One or two sentences.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones — naming the dominant thing others would notice in you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong trait, and you should write the one the facts actually support. A trait nothing demonstrates is a label, not a person.

It may be a contradiction, but only a reliable one, with the facts above showing both halves of it. A contradiction that appears once is not a trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you. It must be a strategy for protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish unconnected to it.

Write it as something you are doing to them, not as a confession. Do not end by naming the thing you are avoiding: the reader already has that field, and stating it again here turns a drive into a summary. Name the behaviour and stop. One or two sentences.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
Same city, same psychology, and the wants have now collided on a third distinct construction.

**The milieu has collapsed back into one place.** Burnaby, New Westminster, East Vancouver, the Lions Gate Bridge, St Paul's Hospital, Windermere Secondary -- one metropolitan area, both lives. The previous run put Lisbon against Bogota and I recorded that as the first real separation in seven pairs. It did not hold.

**Both are the same person in different clothes: the giver whose gift is a leash.** Rizwan hands his sister $327,000 over seventeen years and hates her for continuing to need it. Parvin gives an addict son money, storage, surveillance and legal cover, and hates him for continuing to need it. Both love and hate the same person, which is the design, but both arrive at that person through an identical mechanism -- I gave, you kept needing, therefore I am owed.

**The wants now share an ending, not just an opening.** "... so they never think to ask what you gave up or why you keep touching the scar on your left hand when no injury caused it." / "... so they never ask why you still wear gloves in the room when no procedure requires it, or why you flinch at the sound of doors unlocking." Both close on an unexplained physical tic, introduced with the same "why you [verb] ... when no [noun] [verb]" frame. This is the third consecutive run in which the two wants collide, and the third time on a different construction: the doubled "as if" last run, the ask-then-steer opening before that, the unexplained-tic coda now. Fixing any one of them would not have prevented this.

**Both refusals are the fear of being unnecessary.** "there was no self beneath the giving" / "no proof you matter, and no role left for you to play." That fear has now appeared in both characters of four consecutive runs.

Swap any single detail between these two and nothing would feel wrong, which is the test the guide sets and the test this pair fails.

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The most useful run in weeks, because a pattern I could only hypothesise last time has now repeated exactly.

**The corridor split happened twice in a row, in the same order.** Last run: Tiago left through intent, Carmen left through accident. This run: Rizwan leaves through intent, Parvin leaves through accident. Character 1 breaks the "you did not intend to die" rule; character 2 breaks the accident ban. Two runs, four characters, the same assignment by position.

That suggests a cause I had not considered. **Character 2 is the only one shown the other bio and told not to repeat it.** Character 1 writes freely, reads "your death must come out of a decision you made," and takes the most direct route -- a decision so direct it becomes intent. Character 2 then has to differ from a death that already occupies the decision end of the corridor, and the only unoccupied ground is chance. If that is right, the anti-duplication block is *causing* the accident deaths, and rewording the accident ban cannot fix them, because the pressure is not coming from the ban.

It is two runs, not proof, and 09-20 ran the other way round -- Ravi died in floodwater, Carmen drove a bus into a reservoir. So treat it as the leading hypothesis. The cheap test is to generate character 2 once with the anti-duplication block removed and see which wall its death goes through.

**Second finding: the deaths are inflating, and the ban is why.** Banning accidents pushes toward decisions, and dramatic decisions are easier to write than ordinary ones. Across four runs the deaths have gone: a school bus of children into a reservoir, an overnight drive to deliver a forged letter, a deliberate impact with a toll barrier, and now a forced entry into a correctional facility that opens every cell door on a block. Parvin's cause of death is 171 words against a recent norm of 44 to 68. The ban is not merely failing at its edges; it is changing what kind of death succeeds, away from the ordinary recognisable cruelty the setup prompt asks for and toward spectacle. A rule written to stop cars crashing has produced a prison break.

**One genuine improvement, and it is the one I flagged hardest last time.** Carmen Rojas killed three children and was damned for being controlling. Parvin kills a patient and the Reason for Damnation names the patient. The worst act in the bio is the act she is damned for. Whether that is the note landing or sampling, it is the right direction and it should be protected by whatever comes next.

**Unchanged:** the 110-word cap, breached at 118 and 182. Fifteen of twenty runs on record now exceed it. It is not functioning as a constraint and should either gain a structural lever or stop being stated as a number.

The order of work this implies: test the anti-duplication hypothesis before touching the death rules at all, because if the block is what drives character 2 into accidents, every previous attempt to fix the accident problem was aimed at the wrong file.
